attempts.raw_response: Without additional testing of coding-region markers, the mitochondrial lineage of Paglicci 23 therefore cannot be resolved with certainty. Subsequent studies of other Upper Paleolithic specimens have reinforced the difficulty of assigning haplogroup status from HVR1 alone. The case highlights a broader methodological shift in paleogenetics: early studies relied heavily on the hypervariable regions, but modern protocols increasingly target informative coding-region positions, often through targeted enrichment or whole-genome capture. These advances have allowed researchers to distinguish among H, HV, and U in ancient samples where HVR1 sequences alone remain ambiguous. The Paglicci 23 finding nonetheless remains significant as evidence that mitochondrial lineages ancestral or closely related to present-day Europeans were already present in southern Europe during the Gravettian period, contributing to ongoing debates about genetic continuity and population turnover across the Late Pleistocene transition.

pair.human_continuation:
Haplogroup HV derives from the haplogroup R0 which in turn derives from haplogroup R is a descendant of macro-haplogroup N like its sibling M, is a descendant of haplogroup L3.

MtDNA H had frequency of 19% among Neolithic Early European Farmers and virtually absent among Mesolithic European hunter gatherers.

MtDNA H was also present in the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture.

The clade has been observed among ancient Egyptian mummies excavated at the Abusir el-Meleq archaeological site in Middle Egypt, which date from the pre-Ptolemaic/late New Kingdom and Ptolemaic periods.

Additionally, haplogroup H has been found among specimens at the mainland cemetery in Kulubnarti, Sudan, which date from the Early Christian period (AD 550–800).

Distribution

Haplogroup H is the most common mtDNA clade in Europe.
pair.prefix: In July 2008 ancient mtDNA from an individual called Paglicci 23, whose remains were dated to 28,000 years ago and excavated from Paglicci Cave (Apulia, Italy), were found to be identical to the Cambridge Reference Sequence in HVR1. This once was believed to indicate haplogroup H,  but researchers now recognize that CRS HVR1 also appears in U or HV, because there are no HVR1 mutations that separate CRS from the haplogroup R founder.
